original_value: In today’s digital world, it is common for students to bring their Internet-connected devices to classes. However, using these devices for non-class-related purposes during lessons can be distracting and detrimental to students’ academic performance as well as frustrating for instructors. Defined as the use of organizational resources for work-related purpose (in this case, studies-related purpose; Lim, 2002), cyberloafing has a negative impact on the learning environment as it causes distraction and affects students’ attention and ability to focus. In this study, we examined students’ cyberloafing behavior through the lens of the theory of planned behavior (TPB). We also examined two new constructs, namely class engagement and habit. In addition, this study tested the role of two specific subjective norms, i.e., descriptive and prescriptive norms, in predicting students’ intention to cyberloaf. Data from 238 university students were analyzed with Consistent Partial Least Squares (PLSc) analysis using SMART PLS. Results showed that both habit and intention were significantly related to cyberloafing behavior. Attitude, prescriptive norms and perceived behavioral control were significant in predicting students’ intention to cyberloaf. However, descriptive norms were not significantly related to intention. Finally, class engagement played an important role in determining students’ attitude towards cyberloafing, descriptive norms and perceived behavioral control. In general, results of this study provided support that the extended theory of planned behavior is useful in explaining students’ cyberloafing behavior. Implications of the findings for theory and practice are discussed.

result.paraphrase: In today’s digital environment, it is common for students to bring internet-connected devices to class. Yet using these devices for activities unrelated to the lesson can be distracting and harmful to academic performance, while also frustrating instructors. Cyberloafing, defined as using organizational resources for work-related purposes (in this case, study-related purposes; Lim, 2002), negatively affects the learning environment by creating distraction and reducing students’ attention and concentration. This study investigated students’ cyberloafing behavior through the theory of planned behavior (TPB) and also introduced two additional constructs: class engagement and habit. It further examined the influence of two specific subjective norms, descriptive and prescriptive norms, on students’ intention to cyberloaf. Data from 238 university students were analyzed using Consistent Partial Least Squares (PLSc) with SMART PLS. The results indicated that both habit and intention were significantly associated with cyberloafing behavior. Attitude, prescriptive norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly predicted students’ intention to cyberloaf, whereas descriptive norms were not significantly related to intention. Finally, class engagement played an important role in shaping students’ attitude toward cyberloafing, descriptive norms, and perceived behavioral control. Overall, the findings support the extended theory of planned behavior as a useful framework for explaining students’ cyberloafing behavior. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.
